title: How young people in China lost their community spaces
description:
Back in 2022, young people gathered in the Chinese city of Shanghai for a vigil. It was to mourn the deaths of 10 people who died in a fire in a high-rise residential building in Xinjiang. Many believed the victims couldn’t escape because of strict covid-19 restrictions, although Chinese authorities disputed this.

The demonstrators met on Urumqi Middle Road - a place that would go on to become the focal point of protests known as the Blank Paper Movement. Demonstrations spread across China, with people holding blank white sheets which they said represented “everything we want to say but cannot say”.

Four years later, the spaces young people gathered in are disappearing. Police now patrol Urumqi Middle Road. So what happened to the Blank Paper Movement? Eunice Yang from BBC Chinese breaks it down for us.

summaryZh: 本集 BBC 節目《What in the World》探討中國青年社群空間在白紙運動後逐漸消失的現象。自 2022 年新疆大火引發反對疫情封控的白紙運動以來，中國當局加強對上海烏魯木齊中路等公共場所、酒吧與 LGBT+ 據點的警力監控，導致實體聚會場所大量關閉。BBC 記者 Eunice Yang 指出，許多年輕人轉向使用 Discord 和 Signal 等加密線上平台交流，但在官方審查與監控下，不僅敏感話題受到限制，也難以建立人與人之間的信任感。
summaryEn: This episode of BBC's What in the World explores how community spaces for young people in China have vanished following the 2022 Blank Paper Movement. Triggered by a deadly high-rise fire in Xinjiang during COVID lockdowns, the nationwide demonstrations prompted tighter Chinese state surveillance and police presence in public gathering hubs, leading to the shutdown of many local bars, cafes, and LGBT+ venues. BBC journalist Eunice Yang explains that young people have largely shifted their discussions to encrypted online platforms like Discord and Signal, though heavy censorship and diminished mutual trust continue to pose challenges.
